unit.title: Reading a company's accounts
unit.description: Price and value, income statement, balance sheet, cash, debt and quarterly results

u16l1.title: Price and value aren't the same

steps.title: What you pay and what you get
steps.body:
"Price is what you pay; value is what you get" (Warren Buffett).

• **Fundamental analysis** studies the business (sales, profits, debt, competition) to estimate what it's **worth** and compare that with its **price**. It answers *what* to buy.
• **Technical analysis** studies the chart and tries to answer *when*.

steps.title: Mr Market
steps.body:
Benjamin Graham pictured the market as a moody business partner who offers every day to buy your share or sell you his at a different price. Some days, euphoric, he asks for something crazy; on others, depressed, he practically gives it away.

You don't have to listen to him: his price is an offer, not an order.

steps.title: Margin of safety
steps.body: If you estimate a share is worth €20 and you'll only buy it below €15, you have a **25 % margin of safety**: a cushion in case your estimate is wrong.
steps.key: An excellent company bought too expensively can be a bad investment.
steps.tip: Value is an estimate; that's why you need a cushion.

steps.title: From sales to profit
steps.body:
Panadería Global (a made-up bakery company, € millions):

• **Sales:** 1,000
• − Cost of sales 600 → **gross profit 400** (40 %)
• − Operating expenses 200 → **EBITDA 200**
• − Depreciation and amortisation 50 → **EBIT 150** (15 %)
• − Interest 20 → profit before tax 130
• − Tax (25 %) 32.5 → **net profit 97.5**

steps.title: Margins and EPS
steps.body:
• **Gross margin:** high (60-80 %) in software or luxury; low (20-30 %) in supermarkets.
• **Operating margin** (EBIT ÷ sales): how efficient the business is.
• **Net margin:** what's left for shareholders.

With 100 million shares, **EPS** (earnings per share) = 97.5 ÷ 100 = **€0.975**. The **trend** in margins matters more than any one year's figure.

steps.title: A real case
steps.body: Inditex ended its 2024 financial year with **€38,632m** of sales, a **gross margin of 57.8 %** and **€5,866m** of net profit: of every €100 of sales, just over €15 was profit. It's a figure for practice, not a recommendation.
steps.key: Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity and cash is reality.

steps.title: What it owns and how it pays for it
steps.body:
**Assets = liabilities + equity.**

• **Assets:** what it owns (cash, inventory, factories, brands).
• **Liabilities:** what it owes (banks, bonds, suppliers).
• **Equity:** what belongs to the shareholders.

steps.title: Panadería Global (M€)
steps.body:
**Assets (1,000):** cash 80 · receivables and inventory 170 · ovens and shops 650 · brands 100.

**Liabilities and equity (1,000):** financial debt 400 · suppliers 150 · **equity 450**.

• Book value per share: 450 ÷ 100 = **€4.5**.
• Liquidity: short-term assets (80 + 170 = 250) against short-term debts (150): they're covered.

steps.title: A snapshot, not a film
steps.body: The balance sheet is a snapshot on a specific day; the income statement is the film of the whole year. You need to look at both.
steps.key: What a company owns is funded either by debt or by shareholders' money.
steps.tip: Debt doesn't sink a company in the good years: it sinks it in the bad ones.

steps.title: The three parts
steps.body:
1. **Operating:** the money the business generates day to day.
2. **Investing:** ovens, shops, buying companies (*capex*).
3. **Financing:** debt taken on or repaid, dividends and share buybacks.

steps.title: Free cash flow
steps.body:
**FCF = operating cash flow − capex.**

Panadería Global generates €160m and invests €60m: **FCF = €100m**, €1 per share. That's what it can pay out, use to buy back shares or reduce debt without harming the business.

steps.title: Profit isn't cash
steps.body: Profit counts sales you haven't been paid for yet and deducts expenses that aren't payments (like depreciation). That's why the two can drift apart. Enron, Wirecard and Gowex all reported profits that never turned into cash.
steps.key: Profit is an accounting opinion; cash is a fact.
steps.tip: If profits never reach the bank account, don't trust the profits.

steps.title: Net debt
steps.body:
**Net debt = financial debt − cash.**

Panadería Global: 400 − 80 = **€320m**.

If cash exceeds debt, the company has **net cash**. Inditex, for example, ended its 2024 financial year with **€11,495m of net cash**.

steps.title: How much is too much?
steps.body:
**Net debt / EBITDA:** how many years of EBITDA it would take to pay it off.

• Panadería Global: 320 ÷ 200 = **1.6 times**.
• Under 2: comfortable. Over 4: worrying.

It depends on the sector: utilities, toll roads and property companies can carry more debt because their income is very stable.

steps.title: Interest cover
steps.body: **EBIT ÷ interest** tells you how many times the business covers what it pays on its debt. Panadería Global: 150 ÷ 20 = **7.5 times**. Below 2-3, any stumble starts to pinch.
steps.key: Debt multiplies: good years look better and bad years, much worse.

steps.title: Earnings season
steps.body:
Four times a year, listed companies publish their accounts. Beforehand, analysts publish their **forecasts**: the average is the **consensus** (sales, EPS and what they expect going forward).

The market doesn't compare with last year: it compares with **what it was expecting**.

steps.title: Good isn't good enough
steps.body:
On **12 March 2025**, Inditex reported a **record profit** of €5,866m (+9 %). That day the share price fell more than **7 %**: it was its slowest growth since 2020 and the market found it underwhelming.

And the other way round: a loss-making company can rise if it loses less than expected.

steps.title: What's coming matters more
steps.body: What the company forecasts for the coming quarters (its *guidance*) usually moves the price more than the quarter that has just ended. And these are days of **price gaps**: a stop can be filled well below where you planned.
steps.key: In the stock market, good news that was already expected isn't news.

u16l7.title: Reading an annual report without getting lost

steps.title: Where everything is
steps.body:
An annual report can run to 300 pages. The important parts:

• **Letter from the chair or CEO:** the story. Read it with a critical eye.
• **Financial statements:** income statement, balance sheet and cash flows.
• **Notes:** the detail (debt, lawsuits, adjustments).
• **Auditor's report:** check it has no "qualifications".
• **Risks:** what the company admits could go wrong.

steps.title: Where to find it
steps.body:
• Each company's **investor relations** website.
• **CNMV:** Spanish listed companies (financial information and other relevant information).
• **SEC EDGAR:** US companies (annual **10-K** and quarterly **10-Q**).

Compare at least **5 years**: a single snapshot can mislead.

steps.title: Watch out for "adjusted"
steps.body: Many companies highlight an **adjusted profit** that strips out "one-off" costs. If there are one-offs every year, they aren't one-offs. Always compare with the official profit and with cash.
steps.key: Read the numbers and the notes first; the story, afterwards.

u16l1-1.prompt: What does fundamental analysis try to answer?
options: What to buy and whether it's expensive or cheap
u16l1-1.explanation: Technical analysis tries to answer when; fundamental analysis, what and at what price.

u16l1-2.prompt: You estimate a share is worth €40 and it's trading at €30. What margin of safety do you have on the estimated value?

u16l1-3.prompt: You want a 30 % margin of safety on an estimated value of €50. Below what price would you buy?

u16l1-4.prompt: A great company is a good investment at any price.
u16l1-4.explanation: Anyone who bought Microsoft at its 2000 peak took about 16 years to get back to that price, even though the business stayed excellent.

u16l1-5.prompt: Mr Market is depressed: a company you value at €20 a share is trading at €12 after a general market fall, with no change in its business. What would a value investor do?
options: Check that the business is unchanged and, if so, recognise that the price is well below the value
Buy with all their money without checking anything
u16l1-5.explanation: Graham took advantage of the market's mood swings without getting swept along by them.
feedback: That's it: the price has fallen, the value hasn't. Even so, double-check your estimate.
You'd be selling just when you're being offered a bargain, with no change in the business.
A margin of safety doesn't replace checking your estimate or diversifying.

u16l1-6.prompt: The gap between the estimated value and the price you pay is called the margin of ____.
u16l1-6.explanation: It protects you if your estimate is wrong.

u16l1-7.prompt: Is it about price or value?
options: The company will generate about €100m of cash a year
It has a brand that lets it raise prices
u16l1-7.explanation: You see the price on the screen; the value comes from analysing the business.

u16l1-8.prompt: A share's price and its value can be far apart for years.
u16l1-8.explanation: The price is set by the market's mood; the value, by what the business will generate.

u16l1-9.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Sure, it's already hit the floor
Buy twice as much to average down
First look at why it fell and what the business is worth: cheap isn't the same as undervalued
u16l1-9.explanation: A low price is only an opportunity if it's below the value.
feedback: Something that's fallen 60 % can fall another 60 %.
Doubling up without analysing is just betting more blindly.
OK… and what if it fell because the business is broken? Then the value fell too.
lines: This share has fallen 60 %, it can't go any lower!

u16l1-10.prompt: According to Graham, how should you treat "Mr Market"?
options: Take advantage of his mood swings without obeying him
u16l1-10.explanation: His prices are an offer you can take or leave.

u16l2-1.prompt: Put the income statement in order from top to bottom.
u16l2-1.explanation: Costs, depreciation, interest and tax are deducted one by one.

u16l2-2.prompt: EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and ____.
u16l2-2.explanation: It measures what the business earns before how it's financed and before the wear and tear on its assets.

u16l2-3.prompt: Sales of €500m and cost of sales of €300m. What's the gross margin?

u16l2-4.prompt: Net profit of €60m and 40 million shares. What's the EPS?

u16l2-5.prompt: Inditex had sales of €38,632m and earned €5,866m in its 2024 financial year. What was its net margin? (one decimal place)

u16l2-6.explanation: It measures how much operating profit each euro of sales leaves behind.

u16l2-7.prompt: What does a gross margin that rises year after year usually indicate?
options: That it's going to go bust
u16l2-7.explanation: It can raise prices or cut costs better than its rivals.

u16l2-8.prompt: Quick: which business usually has the lowest gross margin?

u16l2-9.prompt: This is the real price of a share over two months. What trend does it show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u16l2-9.explanation: In the short term, prices are driven by expectations; in the long term they tend to follow profits. The income statement tells you whether there are profits behind the rise.

u16l2-10.prompt: A company can sell more every year and earn less.
u16l2-10.explanation: If costs rise faster than sales, margins shrink. That's why you read the whole statement, not just the sales.

u16l3-1.prompt: Match each concept with its definition.
u16l3-1.explanation: Assets = liabilities + equity: it always balances.

u16l3-2.explanation: What it owns, what it owes and what belongs to the owners.

u16l3-3.explanation: Everything the company owns has been paid for with debt or with shareholders' money.

u16l3-4.prompt: A company has assets of €800m and liabilities of €500m. What's its equity?

u16l3-5.prompt: Equity of €450m and 100 million shares. If the share trades at €15, how many times its book value are you paying?

u16l3-6.prompt: Order from most to least liquid (easiest to turn into money first).
u16l3-6.explanation: Cash is already money; a factory can take years to sell.

u16l3-7.prompt: Short-term assets of €250m and short-term debts of €300m. What does it indicate?
options: It could struggle to pay what falls due soon
u16l3-7.explanation: What falls due within the year is more than what it can turn into money within the year.

u16l3-8.prompt: The balance sheet shows what the company earned during the year.
u16l3-8.explanation: That's the income statement. The balance sheet is a snapshot of what it owns and owes on a specific day.

u16l3-9.prompt: If equity is negative, the company owes more than it owns on its books.
u16l3-9.explanation: It's a serious sign, although sometimes it's due to large share buybacks at very profitable companies. You need to look at why.

u16l3-10.prompt: Pablo compares two bakeries with the same profit. A has €50m of debt and €300m of equity; B, €400m of debt and €50m of equity. A crisis hits and sales fall 30 %. Which suffers more?
options: Both the same: they have the same profit
B: the interest still has to be paid even if it sells less
u16l3-10.explanation: Debt doesn't sink a company in the good years: it sinks it in the bad ones.
feedback: With little debt, A can weather several bad years.
In good years, yes; in bad years, debt makes the difference.
Exactly: debt doesn't wait for the good times to come back.

u16l4-1.prompt: Operating cash flow of €80m and capex of €30m. What's the free cash flow?

u16l4-2.prompt: Free cash flow of €150m and 60 million shares. What's FCF per share?

u16l4-3.prompt: A company invoices €100m this year, but its customers have only paid €70m; it will collect the rest next year. Its expenses, all paid, come to €80m. How much cash has its business generated?
u16l4-3.explanation: 70 − 80 = −€10m. Its income statement may show €20m of profit (100 − 80), but its cash has gone down.

u16l4-4.prompt: Which part of the cash flow statement does it belong to?
u16l4-4.explanation: Day-to-day business, investments and how the company is financed.

u16l4-5.prompt: Rising profits and negative free cash flow for five years in a row. What does it indicate?
u16l4-5.explanation: The profits aren't turning into real money.

u16l4-6.prompt: Free cash flow is easier to dress up than profit.
u16l4-6.explanation: It's the other way round: cash is a fact; profit depends on accounting choices.

u16l4-7.prompt: Laura is analysing a company growing sales and profits by 30 %. But the money its customers owe it has tripled and its FCF has been negative for three years. What does she do?
options: Looks into why it isn't getting paid and doesn't buy until she understands
Ignores cash: what matters is profit
u16l4-7.explanation: When profit and cash drift apart for years, something doesn't add up.
feedback: Growing sales without collecting the money is exactly the red flag.
Good: Gowex and Wirecard had brilliant figures that never reached the bank.
Profit is an accounting opinion; cash is a fact.

u16l4-8.prompt: A retail chain has negative FCF this year because it has opened 200 shops, but its operating cash flow is high and growing. How do you read it?
options: It doesn't matter, cash isn't important
Alarm: it's about to go bust
It may be reasonable: it's investing to grow, as long as the new shops end up paying off
u16l4-8.explanation: Negative FCF from heavy investment isn't the same as a business that doesn't get paid.
feedback: It does matter, which is why you need to understand the reason.
Not necessarily: FCF is negative because it's investing in growth, not because the business isn't generating cash.
That's it: cash that never arrives isn't the same as cash that gets invested.

u16l4-9.explanation: Capex is investment in assets: ovens, shops, machines.

u16l4-10.prompt: What can a company do with its free cash flow? Select all that apply.
options: Count it as next year's sales
u16l4-10.explanation: FCF is money available; it isn't a sale.

u16l5-1.prompt: Financial debt of €300m and cash of €100m. What's the net debt?

u16l5-2.prompt: With that net debt of €200m and EBITDA of €100m, what's net debt/EBITDA?
u16l5-2.explanation: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 times: at the edge of comfortable.

u16l5-3.prompt: EBIT of €90m and interest of €30m. What's the interest cover?
u16l5-3.explanation: 90 ÷ 30 = 3 times: tight. If EBIT halves, it barely covers it 1.5 times.

u16l5-4.prompt: Net debt/EBITDA of 6 times is usually considered comfortable for an industrial company.
u16l5-4.explanation: Above 4 is usually worrying, except in sectors with very stable income.

u16l5-5.prompt: A company with more cash than debt has negative net debt, in other words, net cash.
u16l5-5.explanation: Like Inditex: €11,495m of net cash at the end of its 2024 financial year.

u16l5-6.prompt: Which sector can usually carry more debt without it being worrying?
u16l5-6.explanation: Stable, regulated income makes it possible to service more debt with fewer scares.

u16l5-7.prompt: Net debt of €600m and EBITDA of €200m (3 times). A crisis hits and EBITDA falls to €120m. What's the ratio now?
u16l5-7.explanation: 600 ÷ 120 = 5 times: without borrowing a single extra euro, it goes from acceptable to worrying. That's how debt sinks companies in the bad years.

u16l5-8.prompt: Industrial company: how does its net debt/EBITDA look?
right: Keep an eye on it (2 to 4)

u16l5-9.prompt: Quick: debt 500, cash 100, EBITDA 200. Net debt/EBITDA?

u16l5-10.prompt: Marta is torn between two companies that are identical except for their debt. A: net debt/EBITDA of 0.5 and ROE of 12 %. B: net debt/EBITDA of 4.5 and ROE of 20 %. What should she bear in mind?
options: That debt doesn't matter if the company makes money
That B is better: its ROE is higher
That B's ROE may be inflated by debt and that it will fare worse in a crisis
u16l5-10.explanation: Look at ROE alongside debt: debt inflates both returns and risk.
feedback: It's making money today; the question is what happens the year it doesn't.
Part of that ROE may come from debt, which also multiplies losses when things go wrong.
That's it: more debt, more risk. It's not a better business, just a more leveraged one.

u16l6-1.prompt: The consensus expected EPS of €1.20 and the company reports €1.10, 15 % more than a year ago. What's most likely in the short term?
options: That it rises sharply: it's grown 15 %
That the share falls: it has disappointed against expectations
u16l6-1.explanation: It's compared with what was expected (€1.20), not with last year.

u16l6-2.prompt: Bruno owns shares in a tech company that reports results tomorrow. He's read they'll be "amazing" and wants to triple his position just beforehand. What is he missing?
options: That tomorrow is a bank holiday
That the price already reflects what's expected and it can open with a gap in either direction
Nothing: if they're amazing, it'll go up
u16l6-2.explanation: Before results, the risk is bigger than it looks: a stop doesn't protect you from a gap.
feedback: That's not the issue: the issue is the risk of a gap.
Good: results day is no time to multiply the size of a position.
If "amazing" is what everyone expects, it's already in the price. And if it disappoints, the gap can be huge.

u16l6-3.prompt: Real chart of a big tech company: 30 sessions with no name or date. What did it do over the next 10?
u16l6-3.explanation: Even if you knew its figures before anyone else, you wouldn't know how the market would react: it depends on what it was expecting.

u16l6-4.prompt: Another real share, another 30 sessions. Up or down?
u16l6-4.explanation: Without knowing what the market expects, the chart alone isn't enough to tell what's coming.

u16l6-5.prompt: A company's shares can rise on the day it announces a loss.
u16l6-5.explanation: If it loses less than expected or raises its forecasts, the market may celebrate.

u16l6-6.prompt: A share is at €50 before results and your stop is at €48. It opens with a −12 % gap. At roughly what price is your sale filled?
u16l6-6.explanation: 50 × 0.88 = €44. The stop triggers at the first available price: €4 below what you planned.

u16l6-7.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
right: What the company forecasts for the coming quarters
A jump between the close and the open with no prices in between
The average of what analysts expect

u16l6-8.prompt: Quick: record profit, but below expectations. Most likely reaction?
u16l6-8.explanation: It's compared with the expectation, not with the record.

u16l6-9.prompt: Ana reads "Inditex posts record profit of €5,866m" and is surprised to see the share fall more than 7 %. What's the most reasonable explanation?
options: That the stock market is always wrong
That the market expected more growth and was disappointed by the pace
u16l6-9.explanation: The price reacts to the gap between what happens and what was expected.
feedback: The profit was real; what happened is something else.
It's neither right nor wrong: it compares with what it expected.
That's it: it was its slowest growth since 2020. The record was already in the price.

u16l6-10.prompt: What can move a share on results day? Select all that apply.
options: The forecasts for the coming quarters
u16l6-10.explanation: Anything that changes what the market expects of the future.

u16l7-1.prompt: Put the reading order we suggest in sequence: facts first, then the story.
options: Income statement, balance sheet and cash flows
u16l7-1.explanation: If you read the story with the numbers already in your head, you're far less likely to get carried away.

u16l7-2.prompt: Which are red flags in an annual report? Select all that apply.
options: The "adjusted" profit is very different from the official one year after year
It has changed auditor three times in four years
Free cash flow moves in line with profit
The auditor issues a qualified opinion
u16l7-2.explanation: Cash moving in line with profit is a good sign.

u16l7-3.prompt: Match each document or source with what it is.
u16l7-3.explanation: Knowing where to look saves hours.
right: Quarterly report of a US company
Detail on debt, lawsuits and accounting policies
Regulator where you can look up Spanish listed companies
Annual report of a US company

u16l7-4.prompt: While you read the report, you look at the share price over the last two months. What trend does it show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u16l7-4.explanation: The chart tells you what the price has done; the report, whether the business has changed. A fall with no change in the business isn't the same as a fall because the investment case has broken.

u16l7-5.prompt: "Adjusted" profit is €120m and the official figure is €70m. How many M€ of costs have been set aside as "one-offs"?
u16l7-5.explanation: 120 − 70 = €50m. If that happens every year, they're normal costs.

u16l7-6.prompt: Where do you find the official reports of a US company?

u16l7-7.prompt: To see a company's trend, last year's report is enough.
u16l7-7.explanation: Compare at least 5 years: a single year can be inflated or depressed by a one-off.

u16l7-8.prompt: Pablo reads the CEO's letter: "A historic year, exceptional growth, a bright future". In the notes he finds that debt has doubled and that adjusted profit has been stripping out "one-off costs" for three years. What does he do?
options: Buys because the CEO is excited
Trusts the letter: the CEO knows the company better
Gives more weight to the notes and the cash than to the story
u16l7-8.explanation: Read the numbers and the notes first; the story, afterwards.
feedback: Enthusiasm doesn't pay off debt.
The letter is the story; the notes are the facts. And they don't match.
Good: the numbers in the notes don't come with adjectives.

u16l7-9.prompt: Quick: which part of the report gives an opinion on whether the accounts are reliable?
u16l7-9.explanation: The auditor reviews the accounts and says whether they give a true and fair view.

u16l7-10.prompt: If you only have 10 minutes with an annual report, what do you look at? Pick the three most useful.
options: How sales and profit have developed
u16l7-10.explanation: Growth, cash and debt: the essentials in little time.
